t: Longest Common Subpath — Binary Search Length with Rolling Hashes
o: Each friend travels a sequence of city ids, and we want the longest contiguous city block that appears, in order, inside EVERY path. In Example 1 the block [2,3] occurs in all three routes, so the answer is 2. In Example 2 the singleton routes [0], [1], [2] share nothing, giving 0. Example 3 shows direction matters: [0,1,2,3,4] and its reverse share only single cities, so the answer is 1. Feasibility is monotone — a common subpath of length L implies one of every shorter length — so the answer can be binary searched over [1, min path length], provided each feasibility check is cheap. Total input size is at most 10^5, which rules out comparing raw windows at large lengths and motivates Rabin-Karp rolling hashes.
k: Feasibility is monotone in length: a common subpath of length L yields common subpaths of every shorter length, so binary search applies to the answer itself.
Fingerprint each length-L window with a polynomial rolling hash under two independent mod/base pairs and intersect hash sets across all paths.
With T = total cities <= 10^5, every feasibility check is linear, making the whole algorithm O(T log T).

a.n: Approach 1: Binary Search with Explicit Window Comparison
a.i: Binary search the candidate length L; for each check, store every length-L window of the first path as an explicit tuple in a set, then filter those survivors by scanning each other path window by window. Correct and easy to trust, but each window costs O(L) to build and compare, so large L blows past the limits — it exists to justify hashing.
s: Binary search L within [1, length of the shortest path].
Build a set of tuples for all length-L windows of path 0.
For each subsequent path, keep only windows already present in the current survivor set.
An empty survivor set fails the check; otherwise L is feasible.
Track the largest feasible L and return it.
a.t: O(T * Lmax * log T) — each check builds and probes O(T) explicit windows of length up to Lmax, times binary-search rounds
a.sp: O(T * Lmax) — explicit window copies dominate memory

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search + Double Rolling Hash (Optimal)
a.i: Replace explicit windows with fingerprints: maintain two polynomial hashes (different mod and base) while sweeping each path, producing an O(1)-amortized key per window via the standard subtract-left, multiply, add-right update. Two moduli make accidental collisions astronomically unlikely; combining them into one 64-bit/BigInt key keeps sets compact. Each feasibility check hashes every position of every path once and intersects the sets pairwise, so the entire algorithm is linear per binary-search round.
s: Precompute nothing global; for a given L, compute B^L mod M for both hash families.
Sweep each path maintaining h = h*B + c, removing the outgoing character with h -= out * B^L.
Emit combined key h1 * M2 + h2 for every complete window into a set.
Intersect sets across paths in order; empty intersection fails the check.
Binary search L over [1, shortest path length] and return the largest feasible value.
a.t: O(T log T) — roughly log(shortest path) rounds, each hashing all T window positions in amortized O(1)
a.sp: O(T) — hash sets holding at most one entry per window position

w: Establish monotonicity before writing the binary search — that is the core idea interviewers grade. Pitfalls: paths shorter than the candidate length must fail immediately; a single modulus is vulnerable to anti-hash tests and silent wrong answers, hence double hashing (or verifying a surviving fingerprint by direct comparison); intersect into the smaller set for speed. Deterministic collision-free alternatives include building a suffix automaton of the first path and walking the others, or generalized suffix arrays. Follow-up: reconstruct an actual common subpath by storing one representative start index per surviving hash.
